prop: This design was read against HEAD b995192b1d8ce3828103852a4fd2addd3a6e1e0b on main, with every tracked path unmodified; the only entry `git status --porcelain` reports is the untracked `scratchpad_backup_jps.ts`, which is outside the design.

In Claude Code 2.1.282, a text reply from an MCP tool that carries no `anthropic/maxResultSizeChars` annotation is saved to a file and replaced by a path once it exceeds 50,000 characters. A tool that declares the annotation with value A has its threshold set to min(A, 500,000), lower as well as higher than 50,000, except where a per-tool numeric override (whose source this design did not establish) takes precedence. The documentation states the default in tokens (25,000) and describes the annotation only as raising the threshold; the 50,000-character figure and the lowering behaviour come from the binary.

At the pinned commit no tetel MCP reply is measured before it is sent, so any of these can cross Claude Code's threshold: `look` returns the whole file on a plain open without `lines`, or grep's whole stdout on a search; `run` returns its whole output; `query` returns every fact, claim or prose block in the workspace; and `fact` returns in `folded` the full label of every pending entry. A search's label and its `look` return both end in an exclusion note naming every skipped rendered memo and every git-ignored path, so `fact`'s size grows with the number of searches folded times the length of that note. The `fact` reply carries no captured output.

tetel declares no result-size annotation on any tool at the pinned commit, and the rmcp 3.1.1 it builds against can emit one: the `#[tool]` macro takes a `meta` expression that becomes the tool's `_meta` object in `tools/list`.

Every completed tool result tetel's MCP server sends passes through one site before it leaves: the hand-written `call_tool`, which receives it as `CallToolResponse::Complete(CallToolResult)` from `self.tool_router.call`, with both `content` and `structured_content` in hand. rmcp 3.1.1's `CallToolResult::structured` puts the JSON's serialization into `content` as text and the same value into `structured_content`.

Decision (budget): every MCP reply's content text is at most REPLY_BUDGET = 32768 UTF-8 bytes. A byte bound also bounds Claude Code's own measure, because JavaScript string length never exceeds UTF-8 byte length, and 32768 sits below the 50,000-character default for an unannotated tool, so the bound holds even for a client that ignores the annotation in the next decision.

Decision (declared threshold): every tool tetel lists declares _meta["anthropic/maxResultSizeChars"] = 100000, via rmcp's Tool.meta. That leaves at least 2x headroom over REPLY_BUDGET, which covers the untraced case where Claude Code measures content and structured content together. It is below the 500000 ceiling on purpose: a larger reply costs the caller context even when it is not spilled. Residual risk: a per-tool override inside Claude Code, whose source was not established, would still take precedence.

Decision (backstop): call_tool, which every completed tool result passes through, measures each CallToolResponse::Complete result. When its content text exceeds REPLY_BUDGET, the result is replaced by a text-only reply with structured_content dropped. That reply keeps a prefix of the text, cut at the last line boundary within the budget (or at a char boundary if there is none), followed by a marker stating the bytes shown, the total bytes, and that any capture the call made is intact. Error results are not shaped. This is what makes the bound hold for every reply, including run and check, before their own shaping lands.

Decision (look, path mode): look_path shapes its own reply rather than leaving it to the backstop. When the selected text (the whole file, or the requested lines) would put the reply over REPLY_BUDGET, it returns whole lines from the start of the selection up to the budget and captures only those lines as the pending entry's output. The label names the range actually shown (path lines a-k), so what was looked at equals what was seen, and the reply ends with "shown lines a-k of N; continue with lines k+1-M". If a single line is itself over the budget, it is cut at a char boundary and the label says so. Two alternatives are rejected: an outline, because it needs a parser for every language, and refusal, because it gives the author nothing to work with.

Decision (look, grep mode), adopting TET-56 f3: look_grep still captures grep's whole stdout, because a census has to hold every match. Its printed reply carries whole match lines up to REPLY_BUDGET, and the number of lines and bytes left out is stated in both the printed reply and the label. The exclusion note counts against the budget; when it does not fit, a count-only form replaces it (N rendered memos and M git-ignored paths excluded). Paging a grep is deferred, and the remedy offered in the marker is a narrower root or pattern.

Decision (fact): fact_result always keeps id, action, attention kinds and guidance, and verify. The variable-length lists are bounded: each folded entry, each refused_since_previous_fact entry and each attention extent label is cut to ENTRY_CAP = 1024 bytes with a trailing " …". Whole entries are then kept in order while the reply stays within REPLY_BUDGET, and whatever is left out is replaced by a count and a pointer to query facts. What gets minted is not affected; only the reply is bounded.

Decision (query): QueryParams gains an optional `from` id. facts_text, claims_text and prose_text emit whole records in id order, starting at `from` (or the first record), up to REPLY_BUDGET, and end with a trailer "(showed X-Y of N; continue with from: Z)" whenever records remain. In the listings, extent labels and text are cut to ENTRY_CAP. When `id` is given to facts or claims, only that record is returned with its labels uncut, subject to the backstop. The CLI's query gets the same flags.

prop: Decision (fact): fact_result shapes in a fixed priority order. First, and never dropped: id, action, and the whole `verify` object. In verify, each finding's clause, evidence and why are cut to ENTRY_CAP / 2 = 512 bytes. If a delivered verification's findings still do not fit the budget, verify_block leaves that delivery uncommitted, shows the findings that fit, and states how many were withheld, so the worst case is a finding shown again and never one lost, which is the rule verify_block's own comment already sets. Second, attention entries in order, then third folded and fourth refused_since_previous_fact. Each entry is cut to ENTRY_CAP = 1024 bytes with a trailing " …", and whole entries are kept while the reply stays within REPLY_BUDGET; whatever is left out of each list becomes a count and a pointer to query facts. The guidance text is changed in scope::advice itself, so the MCP reply and the CLI's stderr keep one shared text: it lists at most four extent labels, each cut to ENTRY_CAP, and then a count of the rest. What gets minted is not affected; only the reply is bounded.
why: Attacker a1 round 2: verify_block commits delivery before shaping, so a dropped finding is lost forever; order the lists by priority, keep verify first, and route the attention guidance change through scope::advice itself for both surfaces.

prop: Decision (backstop), a change to call_tool, which today checks build freshness and then returns the router's result unmeasured: call_tool will measure every outcome it returns, including its own stale-build refusal, by C6's measure (content text plus serialized structured_content). A CallToolResponse::Complete result over REPLY_BUDGET, is_error or not, is reduced in two steps. First, if the content text alone fits, only structured_content is dropped. Nothing is lost, since structured() puts the same JSON in the content, and no marker is added. Otherwise, the reply becomes text only: the structured value's `verify` object, if there is one, shaped as C11 shapes it and never cut, then a prefix of the remaining content cut at a line boundary, or at a char boundary if there is none, then a marker, all together at most REPLY_BUDGET, with the marker's maximum length reserved in advance. The marker states only the bytes shown, the total, and that it was the reply that was cut. It says nothing about the call's capture, which is the verb's to report. For an Err(ErrorData), the message is cut the same way. Because every tool call passes through call_tool, the bound holds for every reply, including run, check, claim and prose, before any shaping of their own lands, and a delivered verify finding is never cut away.
why: Attacker a1 round 2: the backstop could cut a delivered finding off an unshaped claim/prose reply; and dropping only structured_content should not print a misleading cut marker.

prop: Decision (fact): fact_result shapes in a fixed priority order. First, and never dropped: id, action, and the whole `verify` object. In verify, each finding's clause, evidence and why are cut to ENTRY_CAP / 2 = 512 bytes. If a delivered verification's findings still do not fit the budget, verify_block leaves that delivery uncommitted, shows the findings that fit, and states how many were withheld, so the worst case is a finding shown again and never one lost, which is the rule verify_block's own comment already sets. Residual: the withheld tail of such a verification is readable only through the CLI's verify-report until a partial delivery cursor exists, which is deferred. Second, attention entries in order, then third folded and fourth refused_since_previous_fact. Each entry is cut to ENTRY_CAP = 1024 bytes with a trailing " …", and whole entries are kept while the reply stays within REPLY_BUDGET; whatever is left out of each list becomes a count and a pointer to query facts. The guidance text is changed in scope::advice itself, so the MCP reply and the CLI's stderr keep one shared text: it lists at most four extent labels, each cut to ENTRY_CAP, and then a count of the rest. What gets minted is not affected; only the reply is bounded.
why: State the residual of the uncommitted-delivery rule: the withheld tail of an oversized verification is not reachable over MCP until a partial delivery cursor exists.

Decision (look, path mode): look_path shapes its own reply rather than leaving it to the backstop. When the selected text (the whole file, or the requested lines) would put the reply over REPLY_BUDGET, it returns whole lines from the start of the selection up to the budget and captures only those lines as the pending entry's output. The label names the range actually shown (path lines a-k), so what was looked at equals what was seen. The reply leads with a paging line, directly under the `==> path <==` header and before the lines, stating the lines shown (a-k of N) and the range to continue with (k+1-M); it leads rather than trails because the backstop keeps a reply's front, so the front is where what was not shown must be said. If a single line is itself over the budget, it is cut at a char boundary and the label says so. Because the CLI's look reaches look_path through the same observe dispatch, the CLI pages and narrows its captures in exactly the same way, deliberately, so that a fact means the same thing whichever surface minted it. Two alternatives are rejected: an outline, because it needs a parser for every language, and refusal, because it gives the author nothing to work with.
why: Slice 2 put the paging line at the front of the reply, not the end (F17): the backstop keeps a reply's front, so a trailing line is the first thing a cut would lose. The design adopts what was built; the line's wording is the code's, not quoted here.

prop: Decision (query), a change to a verb that today has no limit, offset or filter (its only id parameter is read by deps): QueryParams gains two optional parameters, each with one meaning. `from` is always an id. For facts, claims and prose it is the record to start the listing at, and for deps it is the dependent id to start at. The listings keep the order they already print (prose in document position) and emit whole records up to REPLY_BUDGET. Whenever a page is not the whole list, it leads with a paging line, before any record, stating which records it shows (X-Y of N) and the `from` to continue with; it leads rather than trails because the backstop keeps a reply's front. deps pages its dependents the same way. In the listings, each extent label and each text is cut to ENTRY_CAP. A fact that alone exceeds the budget is printed as the only record on its page, with its extent labels kept whole while they fit and the rest replaced by a count that names the call to read them (id: F#, extent_from: k). `extent_from` is a 1-based extent index and applies only with `id` on facts. `id` newly applies to facts and claims as well. For a fact, it returns that record with its labels uncut, paging its extents from `extent_from` with a paging line naming the next index. For a claim, which has no extents, it returns the claim whole. A single label that is over the budget by itself is cut at a char boundary, and the cut is stated. So no query mode on a fact relies on the backstop, and every extent label can be read in full through some page unless it is longer than the budget. The CLI's query subcommand gets the same flags.
why: Slice 3 leads each page with its paging line instead of ending with a trailer (F17), for the same reason as look: the backstop keeps a reply's front. The design adopts what was built.
